title: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)
hook: three days so dark "they saw not one another"; yet in Israel's homes there was light

segments.voice: Yesterday, the portion's first word, bo. Your line was come, not go. Which hard room did you walk into, and did you say it at the door? Today, the ninth plague. Day three hundred thirty-four.

During a power cut at night, the first thing most people do isn't look for a flashlight. It's call out. Are you okay? Where are you? Darkness doesn't only hide the furniture. It hides the people. The ninth plague is darkness, and the Torah describes it in a way that sounds less like night and more like a weight. It came after the locusts, it lasted three days, and the most striking line about it isn't about the sky at all. It's about what people could no longer see in each other.
screen: `THE POWER CUT.` → `ARE YOU OKAY?` → `THE NINTH PLAGUE.`

segments.voice: Moses stretches out his hand toward heaven, and a thick darkness covers Egypt. The old Jewish translation calls it "darkness which may be felt." Darkness you could touch. Then comes the detail. For three days, "they saw not one another, neither rose any from his place." Not just: they couldn't see the road. They couldn't see each other. And because they couldn't see each other, nobody got up. There's a teaching often told in Hasidic circles that reads those two halves as cause and effect. The darkest darkness, it says, is when a person doesn't see his brother. When you stop seeing the person next to you, you stop being able to move. You stay stuck in your place. The verse ends with a turn: "but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings." The Torah doesn't explain how. Commentators offered many answers, and the plain text stays quiet. But notice where the light was: in their dwellings, in homes, among people. The midrash also wonders why the darkness had to last three days, and gives several reasons; none of them is in the verse itself. What the verse does give is the picture: one land where nobody could see anybody, and homes where people could. A dark time can be a whole country's or one person's. Grief does it. Depression does it. A long illness, a lost job. The person inside often can't rise from their place. Someone else, with light, can see them.
screen: `DARKNESS WHICH MAY BE FELT.` · `THEY SAW NOT ONE ANOTHER.` · `NOT SEEING, SO NOT RISING.` · `LIGHT IN THEIR DWELLINGS.` · then, large: `SEE YOUR BROTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for someone in the dark. Settle, and breathe. Let a few faces come to mind, the people in your life right now. Who's had the lights go out lately? A friend who's gone quiet. A neighbor after a loss. A relative who's stopped answering. Let one face stay. You don't have to fix anything. Just see them, properly, the way you'd call out in a power cut. If you pray, you can hold them there for a while. After the bell, send one short message: thinking of you. The bell holds the time.
Bo. Still our portion. Today its ninth plague: darkness so thick no one could see another person, and light in Israel's homes.
Your line: see your brother. Brother, sister, friend, stranger. Today, check on one person who's in a dark stretch, and let them know they've been seen. Day three hundred thirty-four.

screen: `DAY 334 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BO: THIS MONTH IS YOURS (EXODUS 12:1–2).`

howItsDone: The ten plagues are recited at the Passover seder, a drop of wine spilled for each, and darkness is the ninth. Jewish tradition counts visiting and checking on people who are ill or grieving, bikur cholim and comforting mourners, as a mitzvah.

fork.reveal: nobody could see anybody, and nobody moved. a Hasidic teaching reads it: when you don't see your brother, you can't rise.

original.note: Hebrew: darkness. the same word as the darkness over the deep in Genesis 1.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ninth plague was just a very long night.
what it means: a darkness where people stopped seeing each other, and so stopped rising.
what a scholar hears: 10:23 links two clauses, not seeing one another and not rising from one's place; Hasidic teachers read the first as the cause of the second.

notes: JPS 1917 Exodus 10:21 ('even darkness which may be felt') and 10:23 quoted from memory; KJV reads the same. Verify exact wording and punctuation.

The 'whoever doesn't see his brother can't rise from his place' teaching is widely attributed (often to the Chiddushei HaRim of Ger, sometimes others); the script says only 'often told in Hasidic circles'. A Keeper may supply the source.
Midrash on the length and reasons for the darkness (Shemot Rabbah 14; also Rashi on 10:22) mentioned only generally; confirm reference.
Hebrew in 10:21–22 is choshekh; 'afelah' also appears in 10:22. The original game uses choshekh.
Index carry 'see your brother' kept; the carry voice widens it to sister, friend, stranger.
